clinicalPearls: A zoonotic henipavirus (closely related to Nipah virus) reported from eastern Australia, with fruit bats (flying foxes) as the natural reservoir
Human infection has occurred through close contact with infected horses, which act as an amplifying host after acquiring the virus from bat contamination
Presentations range from an influenza-like illness to severe pneumonitis and encephalitis, and a late relapsing encephalitis has been described months to years after the initial infection
The clinical overlap with Nipah virus makes henipaviruses a recognised cause of severe febrile encephalitic illness with high case fatality
There is no licensed specific antiviral or human vaccine; management is intensive supportive care, and a monoclonal antibody has been used experimentally as post-exposure prophylaxis
An equine vaccine is central to prevention by interrupting the horse-to-human transmission chain
Diagnosis relies on RT-PCR and serology performed in high-containment laboratories because the virus requires enhanced biosafety handling
reference.pathophysiology: Hendra virus is a henipavirus maintained in flying-fox reservoirs, which shed virus in urine and other secretions that can contaminate the environment and infect horses. Horses develop severe respiratory and neurological disease and transmit the virus to humans through close contact with respiratory secretions and body fluids. In humans the virus is endotheliotropic and neurotropic, causing systemic vasculitis, pneumonitis, and encephalitis. Persistence within the central nervous system can produce a delayed relapsing encephalitis long after apparent recovery.

Chest imaging and oxygenation assessment for pneumonitis

redFlags: Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal deficits indicating encephalitis
Progressive respiratory failure from severe pneumonitis
History of contact with a sick or dead horse in an endemic region
Neurological deterioration weeks to years after an initial illness suggesting relapsing encephalitis
Any suspected case requiring immediate isolation and notification of public health authorities
reference.prognosis: Human Hendra virus infection is rare but carries a high case fatality, and survivors may suffer neurological sequelae or a late relapsing encephalitis, so long-term follow-up is warranted.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit a horse-contact history in a patient with severe febrile illness in an endemic area
Underestimating the risk of delayed encephalitis after apparent recovery
Handling specimens without appropriate high-containment biosafety precautions
Delaying notification of veterinary and public health authorities to interrupt the transmission chain
Confusing the illness with ordinary community-acquired pneumonia or encephalitis and missing the zoonotic link
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Provide intensive supportive care for pneumonitis and encephalitis, with ventilatory and organ support as needed, as there is no licensed specific antiviral
Consider the experimental henipavirus-neutralising monoclonal antibody as post-exposure prophylaxis after significant exposure
Manage encephalitic complications with seizure control and neuroprotective supportive measures
Apply strict infection-control precautions and personal protective equipment when handling infected patients and animals
Arrange prolonged neurological follow-up given the risk of late relapsing encephalitis
Refer to infectious diseases and critical care and involve public health and veterinary authorities
Prevent human infection by vaccinating horses to interrupt the bat-to-horse-to-human chain and avoiding contact with sick horses
